title: Sprint 3 - Object-Oriented Python
description: Learn object-oriented programming by building a practical Task Management System. Create classes and objects, work with constructors, instance attributes, methods, class attributes, encapsulation, properties, composition, and inheritance.

tickets.title: Create the Task Class
tickets.description: The Developer Utility now needs to manage development tasks. Create a `Task` class that represents a single task with a title and status.
tasks: Create a class named `Task`.
Create a constructor that accepts `title`.
Store the title as an instance attribute.
Set the initial status to `Pending`.
Create a Task object and print its title and status.
learning_objectives: Understand what a Python class represents.
Learn how to create objects from a class.
Understand instance attributes.
Learn how `__init__()` initializes an object.
tickets.evaluation: Creates a Task object and verifies that its title and initial status are stored correctly.
common_mistakes: Using a function instead of a class.
Forgetting `self` in the constructor.
Setting the status outside the object.
Forgetting to initialize the title.
hints: Use the `class` keyword to define the Task class.
The constructor method is named `__init__()`.
Instance attributes are usually stored using `self`.

solution.task.py:
class Task:
    def __init__(self, title):
        self.title = title
        self.status = "Pending"


task = Task("Fix login bug")
print(task.title)
print(task.status)

tickets.title: Add Task Methods
tickets.description: Tasks need to change their state during development. Add methods to the `Task` class that allow a task to be marked as completed and reopened.
tasks: Create a method named `complete()`.
Make `complete()` change the task status to `Completed`.
Create a method named `reopen()`.
Make `reopen()` change the task status back to `Pending`.
Create a Task object and demonstrate both operations.
learning_objectives: Understand instance methods.
Learn how methods modify object state.
Understand how `self` refers to the current object.
tickets.evaluation: Creates a Task object and verifies that calling the methods changes its status correctly.
common_mistakes: Forgetting `self` in method definitions.
Changing a local variable instead of the object's status.
Returning a status without updating the object.
hints: Use `self.status` to access the current task's status.
A method can modify the attributes belonging to its object.

tickets.title: Add Task Priority
tickets.description: Developers need to prioritize tasks. Extend the `Task` class so every task has a priority, with `Medium` used when no priority is provided.
tasks: Add a `priority` parameter to the Task constructor.
Use `Medium` as the default priority.
Store the priority as an instance attribute.
Allow callers to provide a custom priority such as `High` or `Low`.
Verify that both default and custom priorities work.
learning_objectives: Use constructor parameters to configure objects.
Apply default arguments inside class constructors.
Understand how object state is initialized.
tickets.evaluation: Creates tasks with and without an explicit priority and verifies the resulting object state.
common_mistakes: Making priority mandatory.
Hardcoding the priority inside the constructor.
Failing to store the priority on the object.
hints: Constructor parameters work like normal function parameters.
Give the priority parameter a default value of `Medium`.

tickets.title: Create a Developer Class
tickets.description: Tasks need to be assigned to developers. Create a `Developer` class containing a developer's name and role, and add a method that returns a readable description of the developer.
tasks: Create a class named `Developer`.
Accept `name` and `role` in the constructor.
Store both values as instance attributes.
Create a method named `get_profile()`.
Return the developer information in the format `Name - Role`.
learning_objectives: Create multiple classes in Python.
Understand how different classes can model different entities.
Create methods that return formatted information.
tickets.evaluation: Creates Developer objects and verifies that their attributes and profile method return the expected values.
common_mistakes: Returning the wrong format.
Using hardcoded developer information.
Forgetting to store the constructor values.
hints: The Developer class should be independent of the Task class.
Use an instance method to generate the profile.

tickets.title: Assign Developers to Tasks
tickets.description: A task can now be assigned to a developer. Update the `Task` class so that a task can store a Developer object as its assignee.
tasks: Add an `assignee` attribute to the Task class.
Use `None` when a task has no assignee.
Create a method named `assign_to()` that accepts a Developer object.
Store the Developer object as the task's assignee.
Create a method named `get_assignee()` that returns the assigned developer's name or `Unassigned` when no developer is assigned.
learning_objectives: Understand how objects can contain other objects.
Learn basic object composition.
Pass objects as function and method arguments.
tickets.evaluation: Creates Developer and Task objects, assigns developers to tasks, and verifies the resulting relationship.
common_mistakes: Storing only the developer name instead of the Developer object.
Failing to handle unassigned tasks.
Creating a new Developer object inside `assign_to()` instead of using the supplied object.
hints: Objects can be stored in instance attributes just like strings and numbers.
The `assignee` attribute can initially be `None`.

test_cases.input: Task: Fix login bug, Developer: Rahul
Task: Fix login bug, Developer: None

tickets.title: Protect Task Priority
tickets.description: The Task class currently allows any code to directly assign an invalid priority. Protect the priority value so that only `Low`, `Medium`, or `High` can be stored.
tasks: Create a private-style attribute for storing the priority.
Create a property named `priority`.
Allow the priority to be read through the property.
Validate the priority whenever it is changed.
Accept only `Low`, `Medium`, or `High`.
Keep the existing priority unchanged when an invalid value is provided.
learning_objectives: Understand encapsulation.
Learn how Python properties work.
Validate object state before modifying it.
tickets.evaluation: Creates Task objects and attempts to set both valid and invalid priorities, verifying that invalid values do not corrupt the object state.
common_mistakes: Allowing invalid priorities.
Using a public attribute without validation.
Forgetting to create a setter.
Changing the priority before validating the value.
hints: Use a private-style attribute such as `_priority` for the stored value.
A property can provide controlled access to an attribute.
Validate the new value before assigning it.

tickets.title: Track Total Tasks
tickets.description: The task management system needs to know how many Task objects have been created. Add a class attribute that tracks the total number of tasks.
tasks: Create a class attribute named `total_tasks`.
Initialize it to zero.
Increment `total_tasks` every time a Task object is created.
Create multiple Task objects.
Verify that the class-level count contains the total number of created tasks.
learning_objectives: Understand class attributes.
Understand the difference between class-level and instance-level data.
Track shared information across objects.
tickets.evaluation: Creates multiple Task objects and verifies that the class-level counter matches the number of objects created.
common_mistakes: Creating `total_tasks` as an instance attribute.
Resetting the counter every time a Task is created.
Incrementing the wrong variable.
hints: A class attribute is shared by all objects of the class.
Update the counter using the class rather than `self`.

tickets.title: Create a Task Manager
tickets.description: The application now needs an object responsible for managing multiple tasks. Create a `TaskManager` class that stores tasks and provides methods to add and retrieve them.
tasks: Create a class named `TaskManager`.
Initialize an empty list of tasks in the constructor.
Create an `add_task()` method that accepts a Task object.
Create a `get_tasks()` method that returns all stored tasks.
Add multiple Task objects to the manager.
Verify that the manager contains the correct tasks.
learning_objectives: Understand composition between classes.
Store objects inside collections.
Design classes with clear responsibilities.
tickets.evaluation: Creates Task objects, adds them to a TaskManager, and verifies that the correct objects are stored and returned.
common_mistakes: Creating new tasks inside `add_task()` instead of storing the supplied object.
Returning only one task.
Using a global list instead of an instance attribute.
hints: The TaskManager should own a list of Task objects.
Store the supplied object directly in the list.

tickets.title: Create Specialized Task Types
tickets.description: The task management system now needs different types of tasks. Create specialized `BugTask` and `FeatureTask` classes that inherit from the base `Task` class.
tasks: Create a `BugTask` class that inherits from `Task`.
Create a `FeatureTask` class that inherits from `Task`.
Allow `BugTask` to store a `severity` value.
Allow `FeatureTask` to store a `story_points` value.
Ensure both classes retain the behavior provided by the base Task class.
learning_objectives: Understand inheritance.
Learn how child classes reuse parent functionality.
Add specialized attributes to derived classes.
tickets.evaluation: Creates both specialized task types and verifies inherited Task behavior and their specialized attributes.
common_mistakes: Duplicating the entire Task class instead of inheriting from it.
Forgetting to initialize the parent class.
Removing inherited attributes.
Using unrelated classes instead of inheritance.
hints: Use `class BugTask(Task):` to inherit from Task.
Use `super()` when the child class needs to initialize the parent.

tickets.title: Build the Task Management System
tickets.description: Combine the object-oriented concepts learned throughout the sprint into a complete Task Management System. The system should manage developers, tasks, assignments, priorities, and specialized task types.
tasks: Create Task, Developer, TaskManager, BugTask, and FeatureTask classes.
Allow tasks to be created with titles and priorities.
Allow tasks to be assigned to developers.
Allow tasks to be completed and reopened.
Validate task priorities using a property.
Track the total number of created tasks.
Allow TaskManager to store and retrieve tasks.
Support both BugTask and FeatureTask.
Display a summary of all tasks managed by the system.
learning_objectives: Combine classes, objects, methods, constructors, properties, class attributes, composition, and inheritance.
Design a small application using object-oriented principles.
Understand how multiple classes collaborate to solve a real-world problem.
tickets.evaluation: Runs automated scenarios against the complete task management system and verifies object behavior, relationships, validation, inheritance, and task management functionality.
common_mistakes: Putting all functionality into one class.
Using global variables instead of object state.
Duplicating functionality between BugTask, FeatureTask, and Task.
Failing to validate task priorities.
Breaking inherited Task behavior.
Storing developer names instead of Developer objects.
hints: Give each class a clear responsibility.
Use composition when one object needs to contain another object.
Use inheritance when a specialized task should reuse Task behavior.
Keep validation inside the Task priority property.

test_cases.expected_result: Task is created with Pending status and Medium priority
BugTask contains severity and inherited Task behavior
FeatureTask contains story_points and inherited Task behavior
